title: The whole evening
hook: assemble your evening in ten minutes
tomorrow: a man repeats a bedtime prayer back and changes one word. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: together, at a table set and a lamp lit, the evening the good angel blesses. This week brought reading, a kind word, letting go, screens off and a table. Tonight they become one evening.

A good night with friends can leave you buzzing at midnight: dishes in the sink, mind still at the table, replaying every joke. Monks had the same problem, a day full of people and work. So Saint Benedict, writing his Rule for monks, gave the day a door that closes. After supper and a short reading, the monks gather for one last brief prayer, called Compline. Then nobody speaks until morning.
screen: `STILL BUZZING AT MIDNIGHT.` → `A DAY FULL OF PEOPLE.` → `ONE LAST PRAYER: COMPLINE.` → `THEN NOBODY SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Today's question: how does a whole evening end? Benedict's answer has two parts. First, the same words every night. His Rule sets the same psalms for Compline, night after night, and one of them is Psalm 4: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety. Nothing to choose at the end of a long day; the words are waiting. Second, silence. The Rule says monks should love silence at all times, and most of all at night: after Compline, no one speaks, unless a guest needs something or the abbot asks. Nothing is added after it. The day is done. It is still prayed in monasteries, and by some Christians at home from prayer books. Now a neighbor. Sikhs end the day with Kirtan Sohila, hymns of the Gurus from the Guru Granth Sahib, said before sleep. In the gurdwara at night, it is recited as the Guru Granth Sahib is closed and carried to its resting place. What they share is the shape: set words that close the day, every night, so the evening has an ending. And an honest difference. Benedict's Compline is built on psalms from the Hebrew Bible, prayed by a community and followed by a great silence. Kirtan Sohila is the Gurus' own hymns, said at the bedside, and by the congregation as their scripture is laid to rest.
screen: `THE SAME WORDS EVERY NIGHT.` · `THEN SILENCE UNTIL MORNING.` · `COMPLINE: THE DAY'S LAST WORDS.` · `A NEIGHBOR: KIRTAN SOHILA.` · then, large: `MY EVENING.`

segments.voice: On your fingers, walk through tonight's evening in order: three lines read, one kind word, the worry put down, screens off, the table. Close your hand on the last finger, the way Compline closes the day, and keep a small silence, with nothing more to say tonight.
The whole evening: the week's pieces put in order and closed with set words and a little silence, so the day is complete.
The line for tonight: my evening, with an ending that's the same every night. That's the week's evening, whole.

howItsDone: Monks and nuns following the Rule of Benedict pray Compline as the last prayer of the day and keep silence after it; Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep, and in the gurdwara as the Guru Granth Sahib is put to rest for the night.

Compline.meaning: the last prayer of the monastic day, said before sleep

Kirtan Sohila.meaning: a set of the Gurus' hymns Sikhs say before sleep

Guru Granth Sahib.meaning: the Sikh scripture, honored as the living Guru

sources.ref: Rule of Benedict, chapter 18 (Compline: the same psalms every day, 4, 90 and 133 in its numbering) and chapter 42 (silence at night; reading after supper; no speaking after Compline except for guests' need or the abbot's command)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12-13 (Kirtan Sohila); Sikh Rehat Maryada (Kirtan Sohila recited before sleep)
